newsitem.title: USA: GCA April coffee stock data seen mainly neutral.
newsitem.headline: GCA April coffee stock data seen mainly neutral.

text.p: New York coffee futures are likely to be unimpressed by monthly inventory data released late Thursday showing an anticipated increase in U.S. consumer coffee stocks, traders and analysts said.
Supplies of green coffee housed in U.S. warehouses rose in April by 198,000 60-kg bags, to 1,855,000 bags, the Green Coffee Association of New York reported.
Market participants had forecast a build up of between 100,000 and 300,000 bags.
"It is neutral because it is within expectations," said Refco Inc analyst Ann Prendergast. "And it was not up enough to really change the picture of short supply."
The port of New Orleans posted the largest gain in coffee stocks. New Orleans stocks rose by 201,000 bags to 752,000 bags, the GCA said.
Inventories increased by 51,000 bags, to 257,000 bags, in New York. Warehouse stocks in San Francisco also increased in April, rising 18,000 bags to 159,000 bags.
Many market participants had expected the Port of New Orleans to post the biggest increase in stocks, saying heavy shipments of robusta coffee from Vietnam and Thailand accounted for the build up.
While the GCA data does not distinguish origin, some traders said a large increase of robusta coffee would not have much of an impact on the New York market, where only arabica coffee is traded.
"If the majority of the increase was robustas, it does not do anything to alleviate the arabica tightness," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "And that is what's driving this market."

But other industry sources said lower quality robustas were arriving at U.S. warehouses with more frequency because the $1.60 differential between CSCE July arabicas and LIFFE July robustas proved too tempting to many roasters.
"If there's that much robustas coming in then guess what: someone is changing their blends," said one trader. "The high price of arabicas is forcing roasters to use robustas."

Tight supply of arabica beans due to smaller-than-expected crops in many Latin American countries and an increase in consumption of high-quality specialty coffees has been behind coffee futures explosive rally since the end of last year.
On Thursday, CSCE spot May soared 15.55 cents, to 277.05 cents, after peaking at 279.00 cents, its highest level in 20 years.
"The supply situation is real," one trader said. "The trend is higher, higher, higher."
